parts.ask: How do you calculate coordinates from a total station?

explain.say: On a modern building site one surveyor can work alone: a robotic total station follows a prism on a pole, measuring angles and distances to the millimetre. It is a theodolite with a laser rangefinder and a computer inside. Here are its parts, with a beam of light going out to the prism and back.

draw.text: Total stations: distance by light and coordinates by bearing

explain.say: How does light measure distance? The EDM sends out an infrared beam whose brightness rises and falls in a wave, here twenty metres long. Look at the two curves: the returning wave arrives a quarter of a wave behind. If the beam made fifteen whole waves plus that quarter on its round trip, the distance is three hundred and five metres over two: one hundred and fifty two point five.

But how does it know there were fifteen whole waves? It repeats the trick with several different wavelengths, like checking a clock with hour and minute hands. The beam travels along a slope, though. A slope distance of a hundred and fifty point five seven three metres at five degrees up gives exactly a hundred and fifty metres flat and thirteen point one two metres of rise.

Now the magic: coordinates. From station S at easting one thousand, northing two thousand, point P is a hundred and fifty metres away on a bearing of sixty degrees. East goes up by distance times sine of the bearing, a hundred and twenty nine point nine; north by distance times cosine, seventy five. Which way would P move if the bearing were ninety degrees?

explain.say: Due east! Run it backwards and you get stakeout: type in the design coordinates of a column and the total station guides the pole onto the exact spot. Reflectorless models even bounce the beam off a wall. Brilliant! Challenge: from a station at five hundred, five hundred, what are the coordinates of a point a hundred metres away at bearing ninety degrees?

parts.label: Keypad and memory
parts.ask: How do you calculate coordinates from a total station?

faq.a: An electronic theodolite combined with an electronic distance meter and a computer. It measures horizontal and vertical angles and slope distance, then works out coordinates and heights.

Electronic distance measurement sends a modulated light beam to a prism and compares the phase of the returning wave with the outgoing one. Several modulation wavelengths fix the whole number of waves.
asks: How does a total station measure distance?

faq.q: How do you convert slope distance to horizontal distance?
faq.a: Multiply the slope distance by the cosine of the vertical angle. The height difference is the slope distance times the sine. 150.573 metres at 5 degrees gives 150.000 metres and 13.12 metres.

faq.q: How do you calculate coordinates from a total station?
faq.a: Add distance times the sine of the bearing to the station easting, and distance times the cosine to the northing. 150 metres at 60 degrees adds 129.904 east and 75.000 north.

faq.q: What is a reflectorless total station?
faq.a: One whose laser can measure to an ordinary surface such as a wall or rock face without a prism, useful for unreachable or dangerous points.

facts: Erik Bergstrand in Sweden developed the Geodimeter, an early electro-optical distance meter, in the late 1940s.
A typical total station EDM is accurate to about ±(2 mm + 2 mm per km).
